A top 20 hit for [[Tony Bennett]] in its original 1951 version, the song has since been [[Cover version|re-recorded]] many times, with a 1963 version by [[Bobby Vinton]] reaching No. 1.

"Blue Velvet" is a popular song written and composed in 1950 by Bernie Wayne and Lee Morris. A top 20 hit for Tony Bennett in its original 1951 version, the song has since been re-recorded many times, with a 1963 version by Bobby Vinton reaching No. 1.

sections.heading: Inspiration and composition
sections.wikitext:
Songwriter Bernie Wayne was inspired to begin writing "Blue Velvet" on a 1951 visit to [[Richmond, Virginia]] where he stayed at the [[Jefferson Hotel (Richmond, Virginia)|Jefferson Hotel]]. At a party at the hotel, Wayne continually caught sight of a female guest dressed in blue velvet with whom he would have a holiday romance.<ref>{{cite book
| first=Paul N
| last=Herbert
| year=2012
| title=The Jefferson Hotel: the history of a Richmond landmark
| edition=1st US
| publisher=The History Press
| location=Charleston, South Carolina
| page=126
| isbn=978-1-60949-687-6}}</ref><ref name="Indianapolis Star">''Indianapolis Star'' 20 February 1988 "Music's Smooth as Velvet: songwriter touts Greenfield film" by Scott L. Miley p.B-1</ref>
sections.text: Songwriter Bernie Wayne was inspired to begin writing "Blue Velvet" on a 1951 visit to Richmond, Virginia where he stayed at the Jefferson Hotel. At a party at the hotel, Wayne continually caught sight of a female guest dressed in blue velvet with whom he would have a holiday romance.

sections.heading: Tony Bennett original version and 1951 covers
sections.wikitext: The song's co-writer [[Bernie Wayne]] had pitched "Blue Velvet" to [[Columbia Records]] head [[Artists and repertoire|A&R]] man [[Mitch Miller]], who as soon as he'd heard the song's opening measure: "She wore blue velvet", had suggested giving the song to [[Tony Bennett]]. (Wayne's response: "Don't you want to hear the rest of the song?", caused Miller to opine: "Quit while you're ahead!"){{cite book | first=Tony | last=Bennett | year=1998 | title=The Good Life: the autobiography of Tony Bennett | publisher=Simon & Schuster | location= New York, New York | isbn=978-1-4165-7366-1}} Recorded in a July 17, 1951 session with the [[Percy Faith]] orchestra and released September 21, 1951, Bennett's version peaked at No. 16 on the ''[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]'' chart of "Records Most Played by Disc Jockeys","[https://www.worldradiohistory.com/Archive-All-Music/Billboard/50s/1951/Billboard%201951-11-03.pdf Records Most Played by Disc Jockeys]," ''[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]],'' November 3, 1951. p. 34. Accessed October 22, 2015. while reaching No. 18 on ''Billboard's'' chart of "[[Billboard Best Selling Pop Singles Chart|Best Selling Pop Singles]]","[https://www.worldradiohistory.com/Archive-All-Music/Billboard/50s/1951/Billboard%201951-11-24a.pdf Best Selling Pop Singles]," ''[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]],'' November 24, 1951. p. 34. Accessed October 22, 2015. and No. 18 on ''Billboard's'' chart of "Most Played Juke Box Records"."[https://www.worldradiohistory.com/Archive-All-Music/Billboard/50s/1951/Billboard%201951-11-24a.pdf Most Played Juke Box Records]," ''[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]],'' November 24, 1951. p. 42. Accessed October 22, 2015. Bennett's version of "Blue Velvet" made its album debut on a 1959 compilation LP that was also titled ''Blue Velvet.''"[https://books.google.com/books?id=DSAEAAAAMBAJ&pg=PA34 Reviews of This Week's LP's]," ''[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]],'' June 8, 1959. p. 34. Retrieved April 25, 2018. The single's [[A-side and B-side#B-side|B-side]] "Solitaire" was also a Top 20 hit. "Blue Velvet" was expediently [[cover version|covered]] by [[Arthur Prysock]]—whose version although recorded a week after Bennett's evidently was the first version released, in August 1951—[[Bill Farrell (singer)|Bill Farrell]], and Norman Kaye (a solo act who was also a member of the [[Mary Kaye]] Trio): the ''[[Cashbox (magazine)|Cash Box]]'' Top 50 singles chart ranked Bennett's version and the three covers in tandem, with a peak position of No. 12 attained on the chart dated December 1, 1951.[https://www.worldradiohistory.com/Archive-All-Music/Cash-Box/50s/1951/CB-1951-12-01.pdf The Nation's Top 50 Best Selling Records]", ''[[Cashbox (magazine)|Cash Box]]'', December 1, 1951. p. 17. Retrieved April 25, 2018. ''Cash Box'' also ranked Bennett's version as high as No. 11 on its chart of "The Nation's Top 10 Juke Box Tunes".""[https://www.worldradiohistory.com/Archive-All-Music/Cash-Box/50s/1951/CB-1951-12-01.pdf The Nation's Top 10 Juke Box Tunes]", ''[[Cashbox (magazine)|Cash Box]]'', December 1, 1951. p. 4. Retrieved April 25, 2018. ''[[The New York Times]]'' music journalist [[Stephen Holden]] would vaunt "Blue Velvet" as one of the four tracks which defined the first phase of Bennett's recording career: according to Holden "Blue Velvet" along with "[[Because of You (1940 song)|Because of You]]" (1951), "[[Cold, Cold Heart]]" (1951), and "[[Stranger in Paradise (song)|Stranger in Paradise]]" (1953), "stand as the gorgeous final flowering of the high-romantic style invented in the 1940s by [[Frank Sinatra|Sinatra]] [with] arranger [[Axel Stordahl]]. Pure and throbbing, ...Bennett's voice adds a semi-operatic heft to Sinatra's more intimate crooning style. Male pop singing since [the mid-1950s] has never been [so] unabashedly sweet."''The New York Times'' 2 August 2006 "Tony Bennett Turns 80: a rock of eassurance" by Stephen Holden p.E1 In 1957 Bennett would begin a longstanding working relationship with [[jazz]] pianist [[Ralph Sharon]] who Bennett would recall advised him: "If you keep singing...sweet saccharine songs like 'Blue Velvet' sooner or later...you're going to stop selling [records]" and with his 1957 album ''[[The Beat of My Heart]]'' - produced and conducted by Sharon - Bennett had launched a new musical persona as an intensely intimate song stylist.{{cite news|newspaper=Los Angeles Times |date=April 12, 2015 |title=Obituaries: Ralph Sharon (1923-2015) |first=Elaine |last=Woo |page=B6}} A live version of "Blue Velvet" was featured on the 1962 concert album ''[[Tony Bennett at Carnegie Hall]],''{{cite web|url=https://www.allmusic.com/album/at-carnegie-hall-mw0000028741|title=At Carnegie Hall – Tony Bennett|publisher=[[AllMusic]]|access-date=April 25, 2018}} with the selection being included on ''The Good Life,'' a 1963 [[extended play|EP]] release in the UK.[http://www.norwegiancharts.com/showitem.asp?interpret=Tony+Bennett&titel=The+Good+Life&cat=s Tony Bennett - The Good Life], norwegiancharts.com. Retrieved April 25, 2018. Bennett dueted with [[k.d. lang]] on a remake of "Blue Velvet" for his 2011 album ''[[Duets II (Tony Bennett album)|Duets II]],''{{cite web|url=https://www.allmusic.com/album/duets-ii-mw0002184001|title=Duets II – Tony Bennett|publisher=[[AllMusic]]|access-date=April 25, 2018}} while Bennett's 2012 album ''[[Viva Duets]]'' featured Bennett duetting on "Blue Velvet" with [[Maria Gadú]], who sang her part in Portuguese.Lipshutz, Jason. "[https://www.billboard.com/articles/news/480650/tony-bennett-to-release-latin-music-duets-album-in-october Tony Bennett To Release Latin Music 'Duets' Album in October]", ''[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]''.com, August 2, 2012. Retrieved April 25, 2018. ("Blue Velvet" was a bonus cut on an edition of ''Viva Duets'' sold exclusively through [[Target Corporation|Target]].)
sections.text: The song's co-writer Bernie Wayne had pitched "Blue Velvet" to Columbia Records head A&R man Mitch Miller, who as soon as he'd heard the song's opening measure: "She wore blue velvet", had suggested giving the song to Tony Bennett. (Wayne's response: "Don't you want to hear the rest of the song?", caused Miller to opine: "Quit while you're ahead!") Recorded in a July 17, 1951 session with the Percy Faith orchestra and released September 21, 1951, Bennett's version peaked at No. 16 on the Billboard chart of "Records Most Played by Disc Jockeys", while reaching No. 18 on Billboard's chart of "Best Selling Pop Singles", and No. 18 on Billboard's chart of "Most Played Juke Box Records". Bennett's version of "Blue Velvet" made its album debut on a 1959 compilation LP that was also titled Blue Velvet. The single's B-side "Solitaire" was also a Top 20 hit. "Blue Velvet" was expediently covered by Arthur Prysock—whose version although recorded a week after Bennett's evidently was the first version released, in August 1951—Bill Farrell, and Norman Kaye (a solo act who was also a member of the Mary Kaye Trio): the Cash Box Top 50 singles chart ranked Bennett's version and the three covers in tandem, with a peak position of No. 12 attained on the chart dated December 1, 1951. Cash Box also ranked Bennett's version as high as No. 11 on its chart of "The Nation's Top 10 Juke Box Tunes"." The New York Times music journalist Stephen Holden would vaunt "Blue Velvet" as one of the four tracks which defined the first phase of Bennett's recording career: according to Holden "Blue Velvet" along with "Because of You" (1951), "Cold, Cold Heart" (1951), and "Stranger in Paradise" (1953), "stand as the gorgeous final flowering of the high-romantic style invented in the 1940s by Sinatra [with] arranger Axel Stordahl. Pure and throbbing, ...Bennett's voice adds a semi-operatic heft to Sinatra's more intimate crooning style. Male pop singing since [the mid-1950s] has never been [so] unabashedly sweet." In 1957 Bennett would begin a longstanding working relationship with jazz pianist Ralph Sharon who Bennett would recall advised him: "If you keep singing...sweet saccharine songs like 'Blue Velvet' sooner or later...you're going to stop selling [records]" and with his 1957 album The Beat of My Heart - produced and conducted by Sharon - Bennett had launched a new musical persona as an intensely intimate song stylist. A live version of "Blue Velvet" was featured on the 1962 concert album Tony Bennett at Carnegie Hall, with the selection being included on The Good Life, a 1963 EP release in the UK. Bennett dueted with k.d. lang on a remake of "Blue Velvet" for his 2011 album Duets II, while Bennett's 2012 album Viva Duets featured Bennett duetting on "Blue Velvet" with Maria Gadú, who sang her part in Portuguese. ("Blue Velvet" was a bonus cut on an edition of Viva Duets sold exclusively through Target.)

In 1955, the Clovers released a version of the song through Atlantic Records as a single. The song was initially recorded, produced, and released when the R&B group was still composed of John "Buddy" Bailey (lead singer), Billy Mitchell, Matthew McQuater, Harold Lucas, Harold Winley, and Bill Harris. Various members of the group left, died, or were replaced, although the group as a whole still performed the song regardless of whom its members were. The single reached No. 14 on Billboard's Rhythm & Blues Records chart of "Best Sellers in Stores". In 1956, the Clovers released the song on their eponymous album.

sections.heading: The Statues version
sections.wikitext:
The first version of "Blue Velvet" to appear on the [[Billboard Hot 100|''Billboard'' Hot 100]] during the rock 'n' roll era was recorded and released by the Statues, a Nashville-based [[doo-wop]] trio consisting of [[Buzz Cason]], Hugh Jarrett, and Richard Williams.<ref name="StatuesScore">"[https://books.google.com/books?id=wR4EAAAAMBAJ&pg=PA22 The Statues Score with 'Blue Velvet']", ''[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]'', August 29, 1960. p. 22. Retrieved April 25, 2018.</ref> In 1959 Cason and Williams, members of local rockabilly band the Casuals, had been invited by Jarrett, a former member of [[the Jordanaires]] and later a disc jockey at [[WLAC]], to join him - along with veteran background singer and composer [[Marijohn Wilkin]] - to form a vocal chorale who would back artists recording in Nashville;<ref name="StatuesScore"/><ref>[[Buzz Cason|Cason, Buzz]] (2004). ''[https://archive.org/details/adventuresofbuzz00buzz/page/160 Living the Rock 'n Roll Dream: The Adventures of Buzz Cason]'', [[Hal Leonard Corporation]]. p. 160. Retrieved April 25, 2018.</ref> the three male members of the chorale were signed to [[Liberty Records]] by label founder Al Bennett, who had [[Snuff Garrett]] - in his apparent debut as a producer - record the trio in three sessions at the [[Bradley Studios]] at the end of November or the beginning of December 1959.<ref>"[https://www.worldradiohistory.com/Archive-All-Music/Billboard/50s/1959/Billboard%201959-12-07.pdf Music as Written]", ''[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]'', December 7, 1959. p. 35. Retrieved April 24, 2018.</ref>

Two sides from the Garrett sessions had a May 1960 single release credited to the Statues (the group name was a reference to the [[Statue of Liberty]], as the group was signed to Liberty Records): the intended [[A-side and B-side#Double A-side|A-side]] was the Marijohn Wilkin original co-write (with Polly Harrison) "Keep the Hall Light Burning" but it was the [[A-side and B-side#Double A-side|flip]]: a remake of "Blue Velvet", which would not only become a Top Ten hit in Nashville but also rank on regional hit parades across the US rising as high as No. 8 on the September 30, 1960 Top 50 survey for preeminent Los Angeles [[Top 40]] station [[KWVE (AM)#KRLA (1959–2000)|KRLA]].<ref>[http://www.las-solanas.com/surveys/KRLA/KRLA_1960-09-23_1.gif Top Fifty Survey for Week of September 23 to 30, 1960], [[KWVE (AM)#KRLA (1959–2000)|KRLA]]. Retrieved April 25, 2018.</ref> However, the Statues's version of "Blue Velvet" would only accrue enough focused national interest to rank on the Hot 100 for a period of three weeks in August 1960, with a peak of No. 84,<ref>[https://www.billboard.com/music/the-statues/chart-history/hot-100/song/577634 Hot 100 - The Statues Blue Velvet Chart History] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180525031030/https://www.billboard.com/music/the-statues/chart-history/hot-100/song/577634 |date=2018-05-25 }}, ''Billboard.com''. Retrieved April 24, 2018.</ref><ref name="Living the Rock 'n Roll Dream">{{cite book| title=Living the Rock 'n Roll Dream: the adventures of Buzz Cason| first=Buzz| last=Cason| year=2004| publisher=Hal Leonard Corp| location=Milwaukee WI| pages=[https://archive.org/details/adventuresofbuzz00buzz/page/38 38–39]| isbn=978-0634066726| url-access=registration| url=https://archive.org/details/adventuresofbuzz00buzz/page/38}}</ref> while reaching No. 80 on the ''[[Cashbox (magazine)|Cash Box]]'' Top 100.<ref>{{cite magazine|title= Cash Box Top 100 Singles – Week ending September 10, 1960 |magazine= [[Cashbox (magazine)|Cash Box]] |url= http://cashboxmagazine.com/archives/60s_files/19600910.html |url-status= dead |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20121006042635/http://cashboxmagazine.com/archives/60s_files/19600910.html |archive-date= October 6, 2012 |access-date=April 24, 2018}}</ref>
sections.text:
The first version of "Blue Velvet" to appear on the Billboard Hot 100 during the rock 'n' roll era was recorded and released by the Statues, a Nashville-based doo-wop trio consisting of Buzz Cason, Hugh Jarrett, and Richard Williams. In 1959 Cason and Williams, members of local rockabilly band the Casuals, had been invited by Jarrett, a former member of the Jordanaires and later a disc jockey at WLAC, to join him - along with veteran background singer and composer Marijohn Wilkin - to form a vocal chorale who would back artists recording in Nashville; the three male members of the chorale were signed to Liberty Records by label founder Al Bennett, who had Snuff Garrett - in his apparent debut as a producer - record the trio in three sessions at the Bradley Studios at the end of November or the beginning of December 1959.

Two sides from the Garrett sessions had a May 1960 single release credited to the Statues (the group name was a reference to the Statue of Liberty, as the group was signed to Liberty Records): the intended A-side was the Marijohn Wilkin original co-write (with Polly Harrison) "Keep the Hall Light Burning" but it was the flip: a remake of "Blue Velvet", which would not only become a Top Ten hit in Nashville but also rank on regional hit parades across the US rising as high as No. 8 on the September 30, 1960 Top 50 survey for preeminent Los Angeles Top 40 station KRLA. However, the Statues's version of "Blue Velvet" would only accrue enough focused national interest to rank on the Hot 100 for a period of three weeks in August 1960, with a peak of No. 84, while reaching No. 80 on the Cash Box Top 100.

sections.heading: Background
sections.wikitext:
The most successful recording of "Blue Velvet" was recorded (on May 27, 1963) and released by [[Bobby Vinton]] in August 1963, backed by Burt Bacharach and his Orchestra.<ref name="auto"/> Bobby Vinton's version reached No. 1 on the ''Billboard'' Hot 100 on 21 September 1963 and remained at No. 1 for the subsequent two weeks.<ref name="BVH100">[https://www.billboard.com/artist/bobby-vinton/chart-history/hsi/ Hot 100 - Bobby Vinton Blue Velvet Chart History], ''Billboard.com''. Retrieved April 24, 2018.</ref><ref>[[Joel Whitburn|Whitburn, Joel]] (1987). ''The Billboard Book of Top 40 Hits'', [[Billboard Publications]], Inc. p. 316.</ref> "Blue Velvet" also afforded Vinton a No. 1 hit on the U.S. [[Adult Contemporary (chart)|Middle-Road Singles]] chart, where its No. 1 tenure was eight weeks.<ref name="BVAC">[https://www.billboard.com/artist/bobby-vinton/chart-history/asi/ Adult Contemporary - Bobby Vinton Blue Velvet Chart History], ''Billboard.com''. Retrieved April 24, 2018.</ref><ref>"[https://www.worldradiohistory.com/Archive-All-Music/Billboard/60s/1963/Billboard%201963-09-07.pdf Middle-Road Singles]", ''[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]'', September 7, 1963. p. 46. Retrieved May 2, 2018.</ref>

Bobby Vinton's No. 3 hit in the summer of 1963, "[[Blue on Blue (song)|Blue on Blue]]", prompted the recording of the ''[[Blue on Blue (Bobby Vinton album)|Blue on Blue]]'' album comprising songs featuring the word "blue" in the title. Although songwriter Bernie Wayne would recall being told by Vinton that the singer had wanted to record the song since hearing the Tony Bennett version in 1951<ref name="Indianapolis Star"/> it was reportedly Vinton's friend, music publisher Al Gallico, who suggested "Blue Velvet" as a ''Blue on Blue'' album track and sent his secretary with a dollar to a music store to purchase the song's sheet music; an hour later, Vinton had recorded "Blue Velvet" in two takes. Vinton did not expect the song to be a hit, and believed that his remake of "[[Am I Blue?]]" had more sales potential.<ref>{{cite book |title= The Billboard Book of Number One Hits|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=PgGqNrqfrsoC&pg=PT146 |last=Bronson |first=Fred |year=2003 |publisher=Billboard Books |page=137|isbn = 9780823076772}}</ref>

Vinton's version was ranked No. 5 on ''Billboard''{{'}}s end of year ranking "[[Billboard Year-End Hot 100 singles of 1963|Top Records of 1963]]",<ref>"[https://www.worldradiohistory.com/Archive-All-Music/Billboard/60s/1963/Billboard-1963-12-28-II-Whos-Who.pdf Top Records of 1963]", ''[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]'', Section II, December 28, 1963. p. 30. Retrieved February 17, 2018.</ref> No. 4 on ''[[Cashbox (magazine)|Cash Box]]'s'' "Top 100 Chart Hits of 1963",<ref>"[https://www.worldradiohistory.com/Archive-All-Music/Cash-Box/60s/1963/CB-1963-12-28.pdf Top 100 Chart Hits of 1963]," ''[[Cashbox (magazine)|Cash Box]]'', December 28, 1963. p. 18. Retrieved April 18, 2017.</ref> and No. 8 on ''Cash Box''{{'}}s "Top 100 Chart Hits of 1964".<ref>"[https://www.worldradiohistory.com/Archive-All-Music/Cash-Box/60s/1964/CB-1964-12-26.pdf Top 100 Chart Hits of 1964]," ''[[Cashbox (magazine)|Cash Box]],'' December 26, 1964. p. 12. Accessed July 28, 2016.</ref>

Vinton's recording failed to make the British charts when originally released, but the track's being heard in a televised ad campaign for [[Nivea]] [[cold cream]] effected a 1990 UK re-release<ref>''Akron Beacon Journal'' 26 October 1990 "Color Him Back: Vinton's 'Velvet' No. 1 in England" by Mark Faris p.D2</ref> with "Blue Velvet" reaching No. 2 on the [[UK Singles Chart]].<ref name="OCV">[http://www.officialcharts.com/artist/10255/bobby-vinton/ Bobby Vinton - Full Official Chart History], ''[[Official Charts Company]]''. Accessed October 22, 2015</ref>
sections.text:
The most successful recording of "Blue Velvet" was recorded (on May 27, 1963) and released by Bobby Vinton in August 1963, backed by Burt Bacharach and his Orchestra. Bobby Vinton's version reached No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 on 21 September 1963 and remained at No. 1 for the subsequent two weeks. "Blue Velvet" also afforded Vinton a No. 1 hit on the U.S. Middle-Road Singles chart, where its No. 1 tenure was eight weeks.

Bobby Vinton's No. 3 hit in the summer of 1963, "Blue on Blue", prompted the recording of the Blue on Blue album comprising songs featuring the word "blue" in the title. Although songwriter Bernie Wayne would recall being told by Vinton that the singer had wanted to record the song since hearing the Tony Bennett version in 1951 it was reportedly Vinton's friend, music publisher Al Gallico, who suggested "Blue Velvet" as a Blue on Blue album track and sent his secretary with a dollar to a music store to purchase the song's sheet music; an hour later, Vinton had recorded "Blue Velvet" in two takes. Vinton did not expect the song to be a hit, and believed that his remake of "Am I Blue?" had more sales potential.

Vinton's version was ranked No. 5 on Billboard{{'}}s end of year ranking "Top Records of 1963", No. 4 on Cash Box's "Top 100 Chart Hits of 1963", and No. 8 on Cash Box{{'}}s "Top 100 Chart Hits of 1964".

Vinton's recording failed to make the British charts when originally released, but the track's being heard in a televised ad campaign for Nivea cold cream effected a 1990 UK re-release with "Blue Velvet" reaching No. 2 on the UK Singles Chart.

American singer and songwriter Lana Del Rey released a cover of the song "Blue Velvet" in 2012. It appears on her third extended play, Paradise. It was released as a promotional single on September 20, 2012, through Interscope Records, and used in an advertising campaign for the clothing retailer H&M.

sections.heading: Background
sections.wikitext: Del Rey had recorded a cover of "Blue Velvet" for her 2012 [[H&M]] Autumn campaign.<ref>{{cite journal|url =http://www.vogue.co.uk/news/2012/07/17/lana-del-rey-confirmed-as-h-and-m-campaign-star | title =H&M Confirms Lana|date = July 17, 2012 | access-date = September 19, 2012 | first= Ella | last= Alexander | journal = [[Vogue (British magazine)|Vogue UK]]|publisher=[[Condé Nast Publications]]}}</ref> On September 20, the song was released as a promotional single.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.amazon.co.uk/Blue-Velvet/dp/B0098YZQUI/ref=sr_1_1?ie=UTF8&qid=1347790550&sr=8-1 |title=Lana Del Rey: Blue Velvet |date=September 2012 |access-date=September 16, 2012 |website=[[Amazon.com]] |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130509053745/http://www.amazon.co.uk/Blue-Velvet/dp/B0098YZQUI/ref%3Dsr_1_1?ie=UTF8&qid=1347790550&sr=8-1 |archive-date=May 9, 2013 }}</ref> Del Rey was selected for the H&M ad campaign after an impressive performance at a [[Mulberry (company)|Mulberry]] dinner party. Industry moguls Michelle Williams, [[Alexa Chung]], [[Elizabeth Olsen]], and [[Anna Wintour]] attended the party and were impressed by the performance. A public relations manager for H&M said Del Rey was chosen because they "were looking for a style icon and singer to model our fall collection and so Lana Del Rey was the perfect choice."<ref>{{cite web|last=Lee|first=Anne|title=Lana Del Rey treats fashion crowd to Blue Velvet at H&M launch party|url=http://www.metro.co.uk/music/912625-lana-del-rey-treats-fashion-crowd-to-blue-velvet-at-h-m-launch-party|work=[[Metro (British newspaper)|Metro]]|publisher=[[Associated Newspapers]]|access-date=5 October 2012|archive-date=23 September 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120923001235/http://www.metro.co.uk/music/912625-lana-del-rey-treats-fashion-crowd-to-blue-velvet-at-h-m-launch-party|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|last=Nissim|first=Mayer|title=Lana Del Rey unveils full 'Blue Velvet' advert video - watch|url=http://www.digitalspy.com/music/news/a407249/lana-del-rey-unveils-full-blue-velvet-advert-video-watch.html?rss|work=[[Digital Spy]]|date=20 September 2012 |publisher=[[Hearst Magazines]]|access-date=5 October 2012}}</ref>

sections.text: On September 19, the music video for "Blue Velvet", which served as a commercial for the H&M 2012 Autumn Collection as well, was released through H&M. In the video, Del Rey is singing the song in a low-lit room before an audience of pallid people, playing an Americana lounge singer dressed in a pink mohair sweater, She is then hypnotized. Three women dressed identically to Del Rey sit on a couch and watch her coldly. At the end, a little man walks into the room, pulls out the plug for Del Rey's microphone, silencing her. Compared to the David Lynch film of the same name, it was directed by Johan Renck, and composed in post-World War II Americana fashion and the notion of external beauty cloaking inner vulnerability. A behind the scenes video was filmed and posted to H&M's official YouTube channel.

sections.heading: Critical reception
sections.wikitext:
''[[Rolling Stone]]'' called Del Rey's cover "doleful."<ref name=rollingstone/> Carl Williot, of ''[[Idolator (website)|Idolator]],'' dubbed Del Rey's cover "beautifully languorous and dreary (though [it] is replete with her go-to swell of [[String instrument|strings]] and grainy [[Synthesizer|programmed beats]])."<ref name=idol/> Jenna Hally Rubenstein, writing for [[MTV]], called the commercial and vocals "moody, totally broody," playfully adding, "What would a Lana Del Rey campaign be if it didn't make you feel a tad depressed?" In the video, Rubenstein said Del Rey was a "ridiculous beauty" sporting a [[Brigitte Bardot]]–inspired look, which she added, not every singer can pull off.<ref name=mtv/> ''[[People (magazine)|People]]'' said the video was dramatic, intriguing, unique, and played off the moody, vintage [[Cinema of the United States|Hollywood]] image of the retro-inspired starlet. Appropriately, they wrote, the video had [[film noir]] elements.<ref>{{cite web|last=Cress|first=Jennifer|title=Exclusive Video: Behind the Scenes of Lana Del Rey's H&M Campaign|url=http://stylenews.peoplestylewatch.com/2012/09/14/lana-del-rey-hm-campaign-video/|work=[[People (magazine)|People]]|publisher=[[Time Inc]]|access-date=5 October 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151117033929/http://stylenews.peoplestylewatch.com/2012/09/14/lana-del-rey-hm-campaign-video/|archive-date=2015-11-17|url-status=dead}}</ref> Specifically, it was compared to the [[neo-noir]] film, ''[[Mulholland Drive (film)|Mulholland Drive]],'' as well as to the film ''[[Blue Velvet (film)|Blue Velvet]]'' itself.<ref name=artinfo>{{cite web|last=Freeman|first=Nate|title=Lana Del Rey to Channel David Lynch's "Blue Velvet" as the Face of H&M's New Global Campaign|url=http://www.artinfo.com/news/story/814154/lana-del-rey-to-channel-david-lynch%E2%80%99s-%E2%80%9Cblue-velvet%E2%80%9D-as-the-face-of-hms-new-global-campaign|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120720002631/http://www.artinfo.com/news/story/814154/lana-del-rey-to-channel-david-lynch%E2%80%99s-%E2%80%9Cblue-velvet%E2%80%9D-as-the-face-of-hms-new-global-campaign|url-status=usurped|archive-date=July 20, 2012|work=[[Artinfo]]|publisher=[[Louise Blouin Media]]|access-date=5 October 2012}}</ref> In an interview with [[Artinfo]], David Lynch spoke out about Del Rey's cover:<ref name=artinfo/><ref name=nme>{{cite web|title=Watch Lana Del Rey cover 'Blue Velvet' for H&M commercial|url=http://www.nme.com/news/lana-del-rey/66128|work=[[NME]]|date=16 September 2012 |publisher=Time Inc|access-date=5 October 2012}}</ref>
{{Pull quote|Lana Del Rey, she's got some fantastic charisma and — this is a very interesting thing — it's like she's born out of another time. She's got something that's very appealing to people. And I didn't know she was influenced by me!<ref name=artinfo/><ref name=nme/>}}
sections.text:
Rolling Stone called Del Rey's cover "doleful." Carl Williot, of Idolator, dubbed Del Rey's cover "beautifully languorous and dreary (though [it] is replete with her go-to swell of strings and grainy programmed beats)." Jenna Hally Rubenstein, writing for MTV, called the commercial and vocals "moody, totally broody," playfully adding, "What would a Lana Del Rey campaign be if it didn't make you feel a tad depressed?" In the video, Rubenstein said Del Rey was a "ridiculous beauty" sporting a Brigitte Bardot–inspired look, which she added, not every singer can pull off. People said the video was dramatic, intriguing, unique, and played off the moody, vintage Hollywood image of the retro-inspired starlet. Appropriately, they wrote, the video had film noir elements. Specifically, it was compared to the neo-noir film, Mulholland Drive, as well as to the film Blue Velvet itself. In an interview with Artinfo, David Lynch spoke out about Del Rey's cover:
{{Pull quote|Lana Del Rey, she's got some fantastic charisma and — this is a very interesting thing — it's like she's born out of another time. She's got something that's very appealing to people. And I didn't know she was influenced by me!}}

sections.heading: Other recordings
sections.wikitext:
The Moonglows doowop group cover the song on their 1956 Chess Records album, "Look It's The Moonglows."
[[Winley Records|The Paragons]] released a version of the song as a single in 1960. Their version reached No. 103 on ''Billboard''{{'}}s "[[Bubbling Under Hot 100 Singles|Bubbling Under the Hot 100]]".<ref name="Bubbling10360">"[https://www.worldradiohistory.com/Archive-All-Music/Billboard/60s/1960/Billboard%201960-10-03.pdf Bubbling Under the Hot 100]", ''[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]'', October 3, 1960. p. 47. Retrieved April 24, 2018.</ref> It spent three weeks on the chart in the autumn of 1960, sharing the "Bubbling Under" chart for two weeks with the version by the Statues, which had just dropped off the Hot 100 (see Section 4 above).<ref name="Bubbling10360"/>

[[Lawrence Welk|Lawrence Welk and His Orchestra]] released a version in 1963, as a single and on the album ''Wonderful! Wonderful!''<ref>"[https://books.google.com/books?id=TAsEAAAAMBAJ&pg=PA9 Album Reviews]", ''[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]'', November 30, 1963. Retrieved April 24, 2018.</ref> It reached No. 103 on ''Billboard''{{'}}s [[Bubbling Under Hot 100 Singles|Bubbling Under the Hot 100]].<ref>"[https://books.google.com/books?id=YAsEAAAAMBAJ&pg=PA22 Bubbling Under the Hot 100]", ''[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]'' vol 75 #39 (28 September 1963) p. 22. Accessed 15 October 2016.</ref> A different, fully instrumental recording was featured on Welk's 1965 album ''Apples & Bananas''.<ref>"[https://books.google.com/books?id=RCkEAAAAMBAJ&pg=PA55 Recent Stereo Releases for Music Operators]", ''[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]'', September 4, 1965. p. 55. Retrieved April 24, 2018.</ref>

[[Ronnie McDowell]]'s 1991 album ''Unchained Melody'' featured a duet of the song between himself and Vinton.{{citation needed|date=March 2024}}

The 2016 album ''[[Upward Spiral (album)|Upward Spiral]]'' by the [[Branford Marsalis Quartet]] with vocalist [[Kurt Elling]] features a remake of "Blue Velvet".<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.allmusic.com/album/upward-spiral-mw0002939293|title=Upward Spiral – Branford Marsalis Quartet / Kurt Elling / Branford Marsalis|website=[[AllMusic]]|access-date=April 27, 2018}}</ref>

Australian singer [[Kylie Minogue]] recorded "Blue Velvet" and included it as the fourth song in the track list of her 2019 live album ''[[Golden Tour#Golden Live in Concert|Golden Live in Concert]]''.{{citation needed|date=March 2024}}

The Moonglows recorded "Blue Velvet" in 1956, but it was not released for several years.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.45cat.com/record/ch127|title=The Moonglows - Blue Velvet|access-date=3 May 2021|website=45cat.com}}</ref>
sections.text:
The Moonglows doowop group cover the song on their 1956 Chess Records album, "Look It's The Moonglows."
The Paragons released a version of the song as a single in 1960. Their version reached No. 103 on Billboard{{'}}s "Bubbling Under the Hot 100". It spent three weeks on the chart in the autumn of 1960, sharing the "Bubbling Under" chart for two weeks with the version by the Statues, which had just dropped off the Hot 100 (see Section 4 above).

Lawrence Welk and His Orchestra released a version in 1963, as a single and on the album Wonderful! Wonderful! It reached No. 103 on Billboard{{'}}s Bubbling Under the Hot 100. A different, fully instrumental recording was featured on Welk's 1965 album Apples & Bananas.

Ronnie McDowell's 1991 album Unchained Melody featured a duet of the song between himself and Vinton.{{citation needed|date=March 2024}}

The 2016 album Upward Spiral by the Branford Marsalis Quartet with vocalist Kurt Elling features a remake of "Blue Velvet".

Australian singer Kylie Minogue recorded "Blue Velvet" and included it as the fourth song in the track list of her 2019 live album Golden Live in Concert.{{citation needed|date=March 2024}}

The Moonglows recorded "Blue Velvet" in 1956, but it was not released for several years.

sections.heading: Use in film soundtracks
sections.wikitext: [[Bobby Vinton]]'s version is featured several times in [[David Lynch]]'s 1986 film ''[[Blue Velvet (film)|Blue Velvet]].'' The film drew partial inspiration from the song's lyrics, where [[Isabella Rossellini]], who plays Dorothy Vallens, a singer in the film, sings the song in-character.<ref>{{cite web|last=Pelly|first=Jenny|title=Watch: Lana Del Rey Covers "Blue Velvet" in New David Lynch-Inspired H&M Commercial|url=http://pitchfork.com/news/47875-watch-lana-del-rey-covers-blue-velvet-in-new-david-lynch-inspired-hm-commercial/|work=[[Pitchfork Media]]|date=17 September 2012 |access-date=5 October 2012}}</ref> Lynch selected the song, because it conceptually matched the mood of the film. Specifically, in an interview he gave to the ''[[Village Voice]],'' Lynch said of the song: "The mood that came with that song a mood, a time, and things that were of that time."<ref name="villagevoice">{{cite news|last=Borden |first=Lizzie |title=The World According to Lynch |publisher=[[Village Voice]]|date=September 23, 1986}}</ref> Songwriter Bernie Wayne would state that at the film's premiere, he was told by Lynch that when he was a high school student in 1963, Vinton's "Blue Velvet" had been his favorite song.<ref>''South Florida Sun Sentinel'' 24 October 1986 "'Blue Velvet' Enjoys Revival After Film" p.5 (Showtime)</ref>
sections.text: Bobby Vinton's version is featured several times in David Lynch's 1986 film Blue Velvet. The film drew partial inspiration from the song's lyrics, where Isabella Rossellini, who plays Dorothy Vallens, a singer in the film, sings the song in-character. Lynch selected the song, because it conceptually matched the mood of the film. Specifically, in an interview he gave to the Village Voice, Lynch said of the song: "The mood that came with that song a mood, a time, and things that were of that time." Songwriter Bernie Wayne would state that at the film's premiere, he was told by Lynch that when he was a high school student in 1963, Vinton's "Blue Velvet" had been his favorite song.
